failures.evidence: I produced such a moment during a rollout, outside the retention case. A rollout that newly fixes a name another principal already holds: the old configuration fixes nothing for legion-daemon:ACME and the new one fixes it for example-other (C). Live, two broker processes on one database (throwaway probe, $TMPDIR/infra228/probes/r6/zz_tester_r6_test.go on the tester's volume): example-worker (B) claims the name on the old process -> 200, held by B under the ordinary 90-day rule. The new process starts and reserves at its first exchange, logging `left a session name the configuration fixes with its holder until the entry claims it … holder=…example-worker entry=…example-other`. Then B, which no running configuration designates, asks the name on the new process -> 200 and on the old process -> 200; A, also undesignated, -> 400 because B holds it; only when C exchanges -> 200 does it move (holder C, infinity) and B -> 400. So while both configurations run, the name is held by, and answered to, a principal no running configuration fixes it for, and that principal is served rather than refused. The same holds after the last old process stops in my round-5 sequence: the old entry holds the name, no running configuration fixes it for that entry, and it is answered 200 until the new entry exchanges. The bullet's first paragraph does describe this window ('a re-point takes effect at the new entry's first exchange … the previous holder keeps the name'), so no behaviour is undisclosed and no code change is called for; the rollout paragraph's closing sentence contradicts it. Remedy: scope that sentence to what it is true of (for example: while both generations fix the name, it is held by one of their two entries, and any other principal is refused; a name a rollout newly fixes stays with its previous holder until the new entry first exchanges, as above).
